Totally get it—Big O can feel math-y. Here’s a simple way to think about it, plus quick examples you can actually use.

Big picture
- Big O is about how the running time or space grows as the input gets bigger.
- We ignore constants and tiny details. So we care about the shape of the growth, not the exact numbers.
- O(n) = grows in proportion to n (linear). O(1) = stays the same no matter how big n gets (constant).
- Common ones you’ll see: O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n), O(n!).

O(1) and O(n) (the basics)
- O(1) (constant): like “one step” regardless of how many items you have. Example: getting the first item of an array by index.
- O(n) (linear): you do something once for every item. Example: summing all n numbers in a list.

O(log n)
- O(log n) grows slowly because you’re cutting the problem size in half each time.
- Mental picture: you have a phone book and you look up a name by repeatedly splitting the list in half (binary search). Each step halves the remaining search space, so you only need about log2(n) steps.

O(n log n)
- Think of two ideas at once: you do something n times, and inside each of those n steps you do something that costs log n.
- A classic example: mergesort (and many divide-and-conquer algorithms). It splits the data (log n levels of splitting), and at each level you touch every item (n work per level). So total is n log n.
- Another way to see it: T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + O(n) leads to O(n log n). The “log n” comes from the levels of recursion; the O(n) comes from the work done at each level.

Amortized analysis (the long-term average)
- Amortized analysis asks: if I do a sequence of operations, what’s the average cost per operation, over the whole sequence?
- It’s not about a single operation’s worst-case cost, but about the average when you do many operations.

Example: dynamic array that doubles
- Start with capacity 1. Pushing an item costs 1.
- When the array fills, you allocate a new array with double the capacity and copy old items over. That copy costs more, but it only happens occasionally.
- If you push n items, the total cost is something like 2n, so the average cost per push is O(1).
- Takeaway: even though some pushes are expensive, the average cost per push stays constant if you double the size when full. That’s amortized O(1) per push.

A few quick go-to patterns
- Nested loops: if the inner loop runs n times for each of n outer iterations, you get O(n^2).
- Logarithmic behavior: while you halve n each time (n = n/2), you get O(log n).
- Sorting: many common sorts are O(n log n) (mergesort, heapsort, etc.).
- Lookups in a hash table (average case): often O(1) per operation (amortized, if you consider resizing).

Tips to study for the midterm
- Remember the big ones you’ll see most: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2).
- Constant factors don’t matter. Base of the log doesn’t matter (log n is the same class for any base).
- If you see a recurrence like T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n), try to recognize the Master Theorem patterns (helps justify O(n log n) vs O(n^2) vs O(n)).
- For amortized questions, ask: over a sequence of k operations, what’s the total cost, and divide by k to get the average per operation?

The idea in one sentence
- Merge sort splits the array in half over and over until you have lots of tiny sorted pieces (size 1).

  - Finally: [5], [2], [9], [1], [7], [6], [8], [3]

2) Merge bottom level (size-1 blocks into size-2 blocks)
- Merge [5] and [2] → [2, 5]

- Merge [1, 2, 5, 9] and [3, 6, 7, 8] → [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]

Awesome plan. Here’s a clean, intuition-driven walk-through of quicksort, with both the average and worst cases, plus a tiny example.

What quicksort does (the idea)
- Pick a pivot element.
- Partition the array into two parts: those <= pivot and those > pivot.
- Recursively sort the two parts.
- Concatenate (logically) left sorted part + pivot + right sorted part to get the whole sorted array.

Two key ideas that drive the complexity
- Each partition step scans the whole subarray once: O(n) work for a subarray of size n.
- The recursion splits the problem into smaller subarrays. If the split is balanced, you get about log n levels of recursion; if it’s unbalanced (one side tiny, one side big), you get many more levels.

A concrete example (small, with steps)
Let A = [3, 6, 2, 8, 5], and use the last element as pivot (5).

1) Partition around pivot 5
- After partitioning, one valid result could be: [3, 2, 5, 8, 6]
  - Left side: [3, 2] (elements <= 5)
  - Pivot: 5 at its final place
  - Right side: [8, 6] (elements > 5)

2) Recursively sort left side [3, 2]
- Pivot = 2
- Partition -> [2, 3] (left empty, right empty after placing 2 in correct spot)
- Left side now sorted: [2, 3]

3) Recursively sort right side [8, 6]
- Pivot = 6
- Partition -> [6, 8]
- Right side now sorted: [6, 8]

Putting it together: [2, 3] + 5 + [6, 8] → [2, 3, 5, 6, 8]

Why the average case is O(n log n)
- Each partition touches every element in the current subarray once: O(n) per call.
- If the pivot splits roughly in half on average, you get about log2(n) levels of recursion.
- There are 1 + 2 + 4 + ... up to about n elements touched across levels, but the total work is roughly n per level times log n levels: O(n log n).

A quick recurrence view (informal)
- Let k be the number of elements that end up on the left side (0 ≤ k ≤ n-1).
- T(n) = T(k) + T(n-1-k) + Θ(n)  (the Θ(n) is the partition work).
- On average (with a random pivot, or a good pivot strategy), k is about (n-1)/2, so you get two subproblems of size ~n/2 each and the Θ(n) partition work per level. This yields T(n) ≈ 2 T(n/2) + Θ(n) → Θ(n log n).

Why the worst case happens (O(n^2))
- If the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, one side has size 0 and the other has size n-1.
- Then T(n) = T(n-1) + Θ(n), which resolves to Θ(n^2).
- A classic bad scenario: input already sorted and you always pick the first or last element as pivot (if your pivot strategy is not careful).

How to get the good average behavior in practice
- Randomize the pivot: pick a random element as pivot. Then the split is balanced on average, no matter the input order. This makes the average-case O(n log n) with high probability.
- Median-of-three (a simple deterministic tweak): pick the median of the first, middle, and last elements as the pivot. This often avoids worst-case on typical inputs.
- In practice, quicksort with a good pivot is fast and space-efficient (in-place partitioning; recursion stack depth is O(log n) on average).

Space considerations
- In-place quicksort uses O(log n) extra space on average due to recursion stack.
- Worst-case recursion depth can be O(n) if splits are always one-sided, unless you implement tail recursion optimization or convert to an iterative approach for one side.

Why the build-heap step is O(n) (intuition and a tiny calc)

    = n × sum_h (h / 2^{h+1})
    The series sum_h (h / 2^h) converges to a constant (~2). So the total is O(n).
- Intuition that matches the math:
